Four men tore open a roof, to lower their paralyzed friend down to Jesus.
And Jesus did not heal him.
Not at first.
Mark, chapter two.
Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee. Word gets out that Jesus is in the house.
The house fills up. No room, not even about the door.
Four men arrive, carrying a paralyzed man on a mat. They cannot get near.
So they climb onto the roof.
At Capernaum, archaeologists found basalt houses, with roofs of wooden beams, branches, and packed mud.
In Mark's Greek, they dug through it.
Dirt falls on the crowd. And a man on a mat comes down, right in front of Jesus.
Mark says, Jesus saw their faith. Not the sick man's. Theirs.
Everyone waits for a healing. Instead, Jesus says:
Son, thy sins be forgiven thee.
Why say that first?
In that world, sickness was often blamed on sin. A saying in the Talmud: no sick man rises from his bed, until his sins are forgiven.
But scribes were sitting there, thinking: This man speaks blasphemies. Who can forgive sins, but God only?
And they had a point. In Isaiah, God says: I, even I, am he that blotteth out thy transgressions.
Jesus asked them: Which is easier to say? Thy sins be forgiven. Or, Arise, and walk?
Anyone can say forgiven. Nobody can check it. But walk? Everyone can check.
That ye may know that the Son of man hath power on earth to forgive sins, Arise, take up thy bed, and go thy way.
And immediately he arose, took up the bed, and went out before them all.
They said: We never saw it on this fashion.
But that word, blasphemy, came back. At his trial, the high priest used it again. And that time, they condemned him to death.
It all started the day four friends broke through a roof.
